summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client send several commands at once instead of waiting for a reply to each one. A server advertises that it supports this. It makes mail delivery faster, especially over slow links.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking one question and waiting for the answer each time, you hand over a list of questions together, so mail moves faster.

questions: how to send multiple smtp commands at once
what does the pipelining ehlo keyword mean
which smtp commands can be pipelined
subtitle: How an SMTP client may send several commands in one batch instead of waiting for a reply after each.

tldr.problem: SMTP answers one command at a time, so on high-latency links most of the connection time is spent waiting for replies.
tldr.mechanism: A server advertises the PIPELINING keyword in its EHLO reply. The client may then send groups of commands in one TCP send, and the server answers them in order.
tldr.outcome: In the RFC's example the number of turnarounds falls from 9 to 4. It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2197.

today: RFC 2920 is an Internet Standard (STD 60) and obsoletes RFC 2197. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Pipeline SMTP
sections.content:
SMTP has a one-command, one-response structure. On high latency links, the time spent waiting for replies (turnaround time) can dominate the whole connection. Command pipelining batches several commands into a single TCP send operation.

The original SMTP specification, RFC 821, did not say servers must support this, so a non-trivial number of servers cannot handle it. Known flaws include losing buffered input when a connection is handed off mid-dialogue, flushing the TCP input buffer when a command fails, and mishandling failures such as refusing DATA because only the last RCPT TO failed. This memo uses the SMTP service extension mechanism of RFC 1869 so a server can declare it can cope, and clients pipeline only then.
sections.eli5: Some old mail servers get confused if you talk too fast. So the server tells you in advance if it can keep up.

sections.title: Announcing the Extension
sections.content:
The extension is named Pipelining and its EHLO keyword is PIPELINING. It takes no parameter, adds no parameters to MAIL FROM or RCPT TO, and defines no new SMTP verbs.

The client first sends EHLO. If the server replies with code 250 and the reply includes PIPELINING, the server has said it can accept pipelined commands.
sections.eli5: The server holds up a sign saying PIPELINING, which means you may send your questions all together.

sections.title: Client Rules for Command Groups
sections.content:
Once support is confirmed, the client may send groups of commands without waiting for each reply. RSET, MAIL FROM, SEND FROM, SOML FROM, SAML FROM and RCPT TO can appear anywhere in a group. EHLO, DATA, VRFY, EXPN, TURN, QUIT and NOOP can only be the last command in a group, because they change state. NOOP can serve as a synchronisation point.

Clients MUST check all the statuses in a group. Even if every RCPT TO failed, the client cannot assume DATA was rejected. Responses MUST be matched to commands by counting them, never by the error code or text. A client that is not non-blocking MUST check the TCP window size and make sure each group fits within it, which is usually, but not always, 4K octets, or risk deadlock.
sections.eli5: Some questions can go in the middle of your list, but others have to come last because the answer changes what you ask next. You also have to count the answers so you match them to the right question.

sections.title: Server Requirements
sections.content:
A server that offers pipelining MUST respond to commands in the order received. It SHOULD buffer replies to grouped RSET, MAIL FROM, SEND FROM, SOML FROM, SAML FROM and RCPT TO commands so they go out as one unit, but MUST NOT buffer replies to EHLO, DATA, VRFY, EXPN, TURN, QUIT, NOOP or unrecognised commands.

It MUST send all pending replies whenever the local TCP input buffer is emptied, MUST NOT assume anything about commands not yet received, and MUST NOT flush or lose the TCP input buffer under any circumstances. It SHOULD give a positive reply to DATA only if at least one valid RCPT TO was received, and SHOULD make reply text indicate which command it answers. The stated aim is to make conformance as easy as possible for servers.
sections.eli5: The server answers in the same order the questions came in, and never throws away questions it has not read yet.

sections.title: Worked Dialogues
sections.content:
The RFC shows a plain dialogue where the client waits for the server 9 times. With pipelining, the client sends MAIL FROM, three RCPT TO commands and DATA together, then the message end and QUIT together, and the turnarounds drop from 9 to 4.

A second example has every recipient rejected. The client still waits 4 times, and the server answers DATA with 554. A third shows what happens if the server does not check for a valid recipient before accepting DATA: it replies 354, the client sends the dot, and only then does the 554 arrive.
sections.eli5: Mailing three people the slow way takes nine back-and-forths. Sending the questions in batches takes four.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not discuss security issues. It says the extension is not believed to raise any security issues beyond those already present in electronic mail and in fully conforming implementations of RFC 821.
sections.eli5: Sending questions in a batch does not make mail any more or less risky than before.
